pageCache.text:
Welcome from The Headteacher
It is a real privilege to be Headteacher of Brill Church of England School and to lead such a warm, vibrant and caring school community.
Having now completed my first year at Brill, I feel incredibly proud of all that we have achieved together and excited about the journey ahead. Brill is a school with a very special character: our children are at the heart of everything we do, our staff care deeply about giving them the very best and we are fortunate to be surrounded by a wonderfully supportive community.
Our vision: With the wind in our sails, we shall live ‘life in all its fullness.’ (John 10:10), reflects exactly what we want for every child who comes through our doors. We want our children to be happy and confident, to be curious and ambitious, to embrace opportunities and challenges and to leave Brill with wonderful memories and a genuine love of learning.
Our Christian values of Honesty, Hope, Courage and Compassion underpin school life and help our children understand not only how to achieve, but how to grow into thoughtful, kind and responsible young people. As a Church of England school, our Christian foundation is central to who we are, while families of all faiths and none are warmly welcomed, valued and included within our Brill family.
We have high expectations for our children, both academically and personally. We believe primary school should be about far more than what happens inside the classroom. We want to open children’s eyes to the world around them, give them experiences that inspire them and encourage them to be bold, be brave and be Brill-iant.
One of Brill’s greatest strengths is the partnership between our children, families, staff, governors, church and wider village community. By working together, listening to one another and always keeping our children at the centre of our decisions, we can continue to make Brill an exceptional place to learn and grow.
If you are already part of our school community, thank you for being part of what makes Brill so special. If you are considering Brill for your child, I warmly invite you to come and visit us. There really is no better way to understand our school than to meet our children and staff and experience Brill for yourself.
I am enormously proud to be Headteacher of Brill School and very excited about everything that lies ahead.
Mrs Rebecca SmithHeadteacher

Modern Foreign Languages
What does MFL look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, we believe that learning another language helps children to broaden their horizons, develop curiosity about the wider world and communicate with increasing confidence.
Our principal language is French, and children begin encountering the language from the Early Years and Key Stage 1 before progressing into more structured language learning throughout Key Stage 2.
Our MFL curriculum is planned by our specialist MFL teacher specifically for Brill, ensuring a coherent and progressive journey from children’s earliest experiences of French through to Year 6.
In the Early Years and Key Stage 1, learning is delivered by class teachers using planning and resources created by our specialist. From Year 3 onwards, children receive dedicated teaching from our specialist MFL teacher, enabling them to develop increasingly secure knowledge of French pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar alongside the skills of listening, speaking, reading and writing.
We want children to enjoy learning another language and develop the confidence to have a go, communicate and discover more about languages and cultures beyond their own.
INTENT
Our MFL curriculum is ambitious for every child.
We want children to develop a positive and confident attitude towards language learning, building strong foundations that will prepare them for further language study at secondary school and encourage an interest in languages that extends beyond the classroom.
Through our French curriculum, we aim for children to:
We want children to understand that learning a language requires practice, listening, memory and courage.
Getting something wrong is part of learning to communicate.
We encourage children to be bold in using new language, brave enough to have a go and Brill-iant in communicating with others.
speak with increasingly accurate pronunciation and intonation;
develop an age-appropriate understanding of French grammar;
recognise patterns and make connections within language;
communicate for a range of simple purposes;
develop strategies for understanding unfamiliar language;
explore aspects of French-speaking cultures and communities;
IMPLEMENTATION
A Bespoke Brill Curriculum
Our French curriculum has been designed and planned by our specialist MFL teacher specifically for the children of Brill.
This enables us to provide a coherent progression of knowledge and skills rather than treating language learning as a series of disconnected topics.
Learning builds progressively from the Early Years through to Year 6, with vocabulary, grammatical knowledge and language structures deliberately introduced, revisited and developed over time.
Our specialist teacher oversees the curriculum across the school, providing planning and resources for class teachers in the Early Years and Key Stage 1 before directly delivering specialist MFL teaching throughout Key Stage 2.
This provides continuity across children’s entire Brill journey.
Early Language Learning – EYFS and Key Stage 1
Although statutory MFL teaching begins in Key Stage 2, we believe there is real value in giving younger children positive and enjoyable early experiences of another language.
In the Early Years and Key Stage 1, class teachers introduce children to French using planning and resources developed by our MFL specialist.
Learning at this stage is playful, practical and predominantly oral.
Children begin to encounter the sounds and rhythms of French, develop simple vocabulary and become comfortable hearing, repeating and using unfamiliar words and phrases.
Songs, rhymes, games, repetition and conversation help children develop confidence without creating pressure to master formal written language too early.
These experiences establish curiosity and familiarity so that children enter Key Stage 2 ready and excited to learn more.
Specialist Teaching in Key Stage 2
From Year 3 to Year 6, French is taught by our specialist MFL teacher.
Children progressively develop the four key areas of language learning:
Listening – Speaking – Reading – Writing
Lessons provide regular opportunities to hear authentic French, respond orally, practise pronunciation, read increasingly complex language and communicate through writing.
The specialist teaching model enables children to benefit from strong subject knowledge, accurate modelling of pronunciation and carefully planned progression across Key Stage 2.
Building Vocabulary and Language
A growing vocabulary provides the foundation for successful communication.
Children learn new words and phrases within meaningful contexts and are given regular opportunities to retrieve, revisit and apply previously learned language.
As children progress, they move beyond learning isolated words towards combining vocabulary and language structures to create increasingly independent sentences and responses.
Children learn to notice patterns within language and make connections between new and previously learned vocabulary.
We want them to become increasingly able to use what they know rather than simply repeat what they have been taught.
Grammar and Language Structures
Children gradually develop an understanding of how French works as a language.
They encounter age-appropriate grammatical concepts and begin to recognise that languages have their own rules and structures.
As their knowledge develops, children learn to manipulate familiar vocabulary and structures to communicate their own meanings, rather than relying solely upon memorised phrases.
They also make comparisons with English, helping them develop a deeper understanding of language itself.
Speaking and Listening
We want our classrooms to be places where children feel confident to speak French without worrying about being perfect.
Children listen carefully to their teacher, recordings and one another and develop increasingly accurate pronunciation and intonation.
Regular opportunities for repetition, questioning, conversation, games, songs and paired work help children build fluency and confidence.
Learning another language requires children to take a small risk every time they speak.
We celebrate the willingness to have a go.
Reading and Writing
As children progress through Key Stage 2, reading and writing become increasingly important elements of their language learning.
Children learn to recognise familiar words and structures in written French and use their growing knowledge to understand increasingly complex texts.
In writing, they progress from individual words and short phrases towards constructing sentences with greater independence and accuracy.
They are encouraged to draw upon their knowledge of vocabulary, grammar and language patterns to communicate meaning effectively.
Languages, Culture and the Wider World
Learning French is about more than learning words.
Children also develop an awareness that French is spoken by people and communities in different parts of the world and that languages are connected to culture, identity and place.
Through their learning, children encounter aspects of life and culture within French-speaking communities and develop curiosity about similarities and differences between their own experiences and those of others.
This complements our Brill Horizons curriculum, encouraging children to look beyond their immediate surroundings and recognise themselves as part of a diverse and interconnected world.
An Inclusive MFL Curriculum
Languages are for every child at Brill.
Our curriculum is carefully structured so that new learning builds upon secure foundations. Repetition, visual prompts, modelling, actions, songs and opportunities for oral rehearsal support children with different starting points and learning needs.
Appropriate adaptations enable pupils with SEND and additional needs to participate meaningfully, while children who demonstrate greater confidence are challenged to apply familiar language with increasing independence, complexity and creativity.
Success in MFL is not about who can memorise the longest vocabulary list.
It is about developing the confidence and knowledge to communicate.
IMPACT
By the end of their Brill journey, we want our children to be confident, curious and enthusiastic language learners.
We want children to leave Brill able to:
Most importantly, we want children to leave Brill believing:
“I can learn another language.”
We want them to have the confidence to communicate even when they do not know every word, the curiosity to discover more about the wider world and strong foundations upon which their future language learning can build.
Learning another language quite literally broadens children’s horizons – making it a natural and important part of Brill Horizons.
Be Bold. Be Brave. Be Brill-iant.

Music
What does Music look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, we believe that music has the power to bring people together, build confidence, inspire creativity and give children another way to express themselves.
We want every child to experience the joy of making music and to see themselves as a musician – whether they are singing, playing an instrument, composing, listening or performing.
Every class receives a weekly music lesson delivered by specialist music teachers from XYZ Music Academy, ensuring that children benefit from specialist expertise and a progressive musical education throughout their time at Brill.
Our curriculum provides children with opportunities to develop as performers, composers and listeners, progressively building their musicianship, practical skills and musical knowledge.
Beyond whole-class lessons, children can also access peripatetic instrumental tuition, enabling those who wish to take their musical learning further to develop individual instrumental skills.
Music is something to be learned, experienced, shared and enjoyed.
INTENT
Our Music curriculum is ambitious for every child.
We want children to develop the knowledge, skills and confidence to participate actively in music and to appreciate music in its many forms.
Through our Music curriculum, we aim for children to:
We want children to understand that becoming a musician involves listening, practising, experimenting, collaborating and performing.
We encourage children to be bold in expressing themselves, brave enough to perform and Brill-iant in making music together.
develop confidence and enjoyment in singing;
improvise and compose their own music;
understand and use musical notation progressively;
listen carefully and respond thoughtfully to music;
develop and use appropriate musical vocabulary;
learn about significant composers, performers and musicians;
perform individually and collaboratively;
IMPLEMENTATION
Specialist Music Teaching
Music at Brill is taught by specialist teachers from XYZ Music Academy.
Every class receives a dedicated music lesson each week, giving children consistent access to high-quality specialist teaching throughout the year.
The XYZ curriculum is aligned with the Model Music Curriculum and provides progressive learning from the Early Years through to Year 6. Children build musical confidence through active participation, with opportunities to sing, compose, listen, perform and develop musicianship.
As children progress, their learning becomes increasingly sophisticated, enabling them to build upon previous musical knowledge and apply it with greater independence and confidence.
Singing and Musicianship
Singing is an important part of musical life at Brill.
Children develop their voices progressively, learning to sing with increasing awareness of pitch, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, phrasing and expression.
Singing together also teaches children to listen to one another and understand the importance of their own contribution within a larger group.
Through musicianship activities, children develop their understanding of the fundamental elements of music and learn the vocabulary needed to talk and think about music with increasing precision.
XYZ’s programme progressively develops children’s confidence as performers, music-creators and audiences, moving from exploration and experimentation in the early years towards increasingly sophisticated musical understanding.
Playing and Performing
Children have regular opportunities to make music practically.
Throughout their time at Brill, they encounter both rhythmic and melodic instruments, developing increasing control and musical understanding.
The XYZ programme provides opportunities to experience instruments and approaches including percussion, body percussion, recorder, keyboard, ukulele and xylophone as children progress through the curriculum.
Children learn to play individually and collaboratively, listen to others, maintain their own part and contribute to an ensemble.
We want children to experience the particular sense of achievement that comes from making music together.
Composing and Creating
Children are not only taught to perform music created by others – they learn to create music of their own.
From experimenting with sounds and simple rhythmic patterns to increasingly sophisticated improvisation and composition, children learn how musical ideas can be created, developed, recorded and refined.
As they progress through school, children develop their understanding of rhythm, melody, structure, notation and the elements of music, using this knowledge to make increasingly purposeful compositional choices.
Creativity is encouraged alongside musical knowledge: children are given opportunities to explore ideas, take appropriate creative risks and discover that there can be many different musical responses to the same starting point.
Listening and Musical Appreciation
Listening is fundamental to becoming a musician.
Children encounter music from a wide range of genres, styles, periods and traditions, developing their ability to listen actively and respond using increasingly sophisticated musical vocabulary.
They learn about significant composers, musicians and performers and explore how music has developed and been influenced by its historical, social and cultural context.
As children progress through Key Stage 2, XYZ’s curriculum develops this further through music history and encounters with an inclusive range of composers and performers from different backgrounds and musical traditions.
We want children to leave Brill willing to listen beyond the music they already know and to be curious about the extraordinary variety of music in the world.
Music Beyond the Classroom
Music has an important place in the wider life of Brill School.
Children have opportunities to sing and perform together, share their musical achievements and perform for others, including through school assemblies and other performance opportunities.
We want performance to feel like a natural part of musical learning rather than something reserved only for the most confident musicians.
Children are encouraged to have a go, share what they have learned and celebrate one another’s achievements.
These experiences help develop not only musical ability but also confidence, courage, collaboration and a sense of belonging.
Individual Instrumental Tuition
For children who wish to develop their musical interests further, peripatetic instrumental lessons are available at Brill.
These lessons provide opportunities for children to receive more focused tuition and develop their technique and musicianship on an individual instrument.
Together with our whole-class provision, this enables children to discover musical interests and talents which they may choose to pursue beyond the primary years.
Music and Our Brill Values
Music provides wonderful opportunities to live out our values of Honesty, Hope, Courage and Compassion.
It takes Courage to perform in front of others.
It takes Hope and perseverance to practise something that cannot yet be played.
It takes Honesty to listen critically to our own performance and recognise how we can improve.
And it takes Compassion to listen, collaborate, encourage others and celebrate somebody else’s success.
Music reminds children that individual voices matter – but that something particularly powerful can happen when those voices come together.
An Inclusive Music Curriculum
Music is for every child at Brill.
Our specialist provision enables children with different starting points, experiences and levels of musical confidence to participate and progress.
Activities and resources can be adapted to support pupils with SEND and additional needs, while children demonstrating greater musical proficiency can access increased challenge and complexity. XYZ’s programme is specifically designed to enable children with different levels of prior attainment to participate while maintaining high expectations.
We want every child to experience the enjoyment and sense of achievement that comes from making music successfully.
IMPACT
By the end of their Brill journey, we want our children to see themselves as confident, creative and enthusiastic musicians.
We want children to leave Brill able to:
Most importantly, we want children to leave Brill having experienced the joy of making music.
For some, this may inspire a lifelong passion, further instrumental study or future musical achievement. For others, it may simply mean having the confidence to sing, listen, perform and enjoy music.
We want every Brill child to know that music belongs to them and that their voice has a place within it.
Be Bold. Be Brave. Be Brill-iant.

Governors
Brill C of E School is a single academy Trust school. This means we are state-funded schools but independent from local authorities- meaning we aren’t run by the council. This gives us more freedom to decide on own curriculums, term dates, school hours and how we spend our money. We are regulated by Ofsted and adhere to stringent financial controls to ensure that we provide value for money. The day to day running of the school is managed by the Headteacher and this is overseen by our School Governors who are all volunteers.
What do Governors do?
Governors have three main functions:
Governors also ensure the school’s safeguarding measures are safe and effective.
We meet as a full governing board three times a year, and then have a day long strategy session in the summer term to look forward 3-5 years and set goals.
We have two committees. These oversee different aspects of the school’s work and meet every half term.
The Education and Standards Committee monitors children’s attainment and progress, the school curriculum and approach. As part of this we visit school where we work with subject leaders, talk to children and look at books to understand the impact of the curriculum and the school’s development plan for each year.
The Resources Committee monitors how the school delivers education including: how the school uses funds and ensures rigorous financial management; recruiting, developing and retaining an outstanding staff team, and ongoing development and maintenance of a safe, inspiring learning environment.
Each governor has a role within these committees and also works with a link staff member on one of our strategic priorities each year. You can contact governors via the school office or on the emails below.

Art and Design
What does Art look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, we believe that Art gives children the opportunity to observe, imagine, experiment and express ideas in ways that are uniquely their own.
We want every child to see themselves as an artist: someone who can explore ideas, develop skills, make creative choices and respond thoughtfully to the world around them.
Art and Design forms part of our Brill Horizons curriculum and is supported by Cornerstones Maestro, providing a carefully sequenced progression of artistic knowledge and skills from the Early Years through to Year 6.
Throughout their journey at Brill, children encounter a rich range of artists, designers, movements, techniques and creative traditions. They learn to work confidently with different materials and processes while developing their own ideas and increasingly individual artistic voice.
We want children to understand that Art is not about everybody producing the same finished piece. It is about looking closely, thinking creatively, experimenting bravely and making purposeful choices.
INTENT
Our Art and Design curriculum is ambitious for every child.
We want children to develop the knowledge, skills, confidence and curiosity to create, explore and respond to art.
Children progressively develop their understanding of drawing, painting, colour, print, pattern, texture, form and three-dimensional work, encountering a range of media, materials and techniques as they move through the school.
Alongside practical skills, children learn about artists and creative traditions from different periods, cultures and communities, exploring how and why art is created.
Through our Art curriculum, we aim for children to:
We want children to recognise that creativity involves curiosity, experimentation and courage.
Not every idea will work. Not every mark needs to be perfect. Sometimes the most interesting creative discoveries happen when children are willing to experiment.
We encourage children to be bold in their ideas, brave in experimenting and Brill-iant in expressing their creativity.

IMPLEMENTATION
Brill Horizons and Cornerstones Maestro
Art and Design is taught through our Brill Horizons curriculum, supported by Cornerstones Maestro.
Learning is carefully sequenced so that children’s artistic knowledge, techniques and understanding develop progressively from their earliest creative experiences in the Early Years through to increasingly sophisticated and independent work in Year 6.
Children revisit important techniques and concepts, allowing them to practise, refine and apply what they have previously learned in new contexts.
Our Brill Horizons Big Ideas provide natural connections within Art, particularly:
Creativity – exploring and expressing original ideas;
Materials – understanding the possibilities and limitations of different media;
Processes – learning and refining artistic techniques;
Comparison – considering different artists, approaches and creative responses;
Significance – understanding influential artists, artworks and creative movements; and
Change – recognising how ideas and artwork develop and evolve.
These recurring ideas help children recognise that becoming an artist is a process of learning, experimenting, reflecting and developing.
Developing Artistic Knowledge and Skills
Children are explicitly taught the knowledge and techniques they need to become increasingly confident artists.
Throughout their Brill journey, they have opportunities to develop and refine skills across areas including:
Teachers model techniques and introduce children to the properties and possibilities of different media and materials.
As children progress, they are expected to use this growing repertoire with increasing control, confidence and independence.
The ultimate aim is not simply for children to know how to use a particular technique, but to be able to decide when and why they might choose to use it.

We want children to understand that a sketchbook does not need to be filled with polished, finished pieces.
It is a working space for curiosity, experimentation and creative thinking.

Artists, Designers and Creative Traditions

We want children to be inspired by artists while developing ideas that increasingly become their own.
Looking, Talking and Responding to Art
Art is both something we create and something we experience.
Children are encouraged to look closely at artwork and develop the vocabulary and confidence to discuss what they notice.
They learn that responses to art can be personal and that different people may interpret the same artwork in different ways.
Children are encouraged to explain their responses and listen respectfully to the interpretations of others.
As their knowledge develops, they become increasingly able to discuss technique, media, composition, style, purpose and artistic choices, moving beyond simply saying whether they like or dislike a piece.
Creativity and Individual Expression
While children need secure knowledge and skills, we also want Art at Brill to provide genuine opportunities for individual creativity.
Children are encouraged to explore possibilities and make decisions about their work rather than simply following identical step-by-step instructions towards the same outcome.
As their technical confidence develops, they are given increasing freedom to select and combine ideas, materials and techniques.
We want a classroom full of children’s artwork to demonstrate shared learning but individual responses.
Art provides children with a powerful opportunity to communicate ideas, experiences and emotions that may not always be easily expressed through words.
Every child’s creative voice is valued.
Our Environment as Inspiration
Our beautiful rural location provides a rich source of artistic inspiration.
Our school grounds, village and surrounding natural environment give children opportunities to observe colour, shape, pattern, texture, light and seasonal change first-hand.
Where appropriate, children use their environment as a starting point for observation, drawing, photography, pattern, colour and creative exploration.
Art encourages children to slow down and notice – to look more carefully at things they might otherwise pass by.
This connection with our surroundings helps children appreciate both the creativity of others and the beauty and detail within the world around them.
Evaluating and Refining
Artists rarely create their final piece immediately.
Children learn that artwork develops through a process of exploration, decision-making, reflection and refinement.
They are encouraged to talk about their work, consider what has been successful and identify what they might develop or change.
As children become older, evaluation becomes increasingly thoughtful and informed by their growing artistic knowledge.
Feedback is used positively, while recognising that artistic decisions are not always about finding one single “correct” answer.
Children learn to make changes because they have a reason for doing so, developing greater ownership of their creative process.
An Inclusive Art Curriculum
Art is for every child at Brill.
We recognise that children bring different experiences, strengths and levels of confidence to creative learning.
Teachers use appropriate adaptations, modelling, resources and equipment to enable all pupils, including those with SEND and additional needs, to participate meaningfully and experience success.
Art can provide particularly powerful opportunities for children to communicate and demonstrate strengths in different ways.
Children who demonstrate secure artistic knowledge and skill are challenged through increasing independence, experimentation, technical sophistication and creative decision-making, rather than simply being expected to produce more work.

Art naturally connects with learning across our Brill Horizons curriculum.
History provides opportunities to explore art as evidence of different times and societies. Geography introduces children to different places, cultures and landscapes. Science encourages close observation of the natural world, while Design and Technology provides opportunities to apply creativity to purposeful design.
RE can introduce children to art, architecture and symbolism connected with different faith traditions, while English provides rich inspiration through stories, poetry and imagination.
These connections enable children to understand that art has always been an important way in which humans record, communicate, question, celebrate and make sense of their world.

We want them to notice beauty and detail, appreciate the creativity of others and have the courage to create something that is distinctly their own.

Computing
What does Computing look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, we want children to become confident, creative and responsible users of technology who understand not only how to use digital tools, but how and why technology works.
Computing is an important part of our Brill Horizons curriculum, supported by Cornerstones Maestro and Barefoot Computing. Together, these provide a carefully sequenced approach through which children progressively develop their knowledge and skills across computer science, information technology and digital literacy.
Technology will form an important part of our children’s futures. We therefore want them to be able to use it purposefully, safely and intelligently – as creators and problem-solvers rather than simply consumers.
From exploring algorithms and programming to creating digital content, handling information and understanding online safety, children develop the knowledge and confidence they need to navigate an increasingly digital world.
INTENT
Our Computing curriculum is ambitious for every child.
We want children to develop the knowledge and skills to understand, create and communicate using technology, alongside the critical thinking needed to make safe and responsible choices in the digital world.
Through our Computing curriculum, we aim for children to:
We want children to understand that Computing isn’t simply about knowing which button to press.
It is about thinking logically, solving problems, creating, questioning and making informed choices.
We encourage children to be bold in exploring possibilities, brave when solving problems and Brill-iant in using technology creatively and responsibly.
understand the fundamental principles of computer science;
develop computational thinking and logical reasoning;
understand and create algorithms;
recognise patterns and solve problems systematically;
select appropriate technology for different tasks;
understand how digital systems and networks work;
develop confidence when encountering unfamiliar technology;
become thoughtful and responsible digital citizens.
IMPLEMENTATION
Brill Horizons, Maestro and Barefoot Computing
Computing is taught through our Brill Horizons curriculum, with learning supported by Cornerstones Maestro and Barefoot Computing.
Learning is carefully sequenced so that children’s knowledge and skills develop progressively from their earliest experiences with technology through to increasingly sophisticated computing in Key Stage 2.
Barefoot Computing supports the development of computational thinking, helping children learn to approach problems logically and systematically.
Children develop important ways of thinking including:
Logic – predicting and analysing what might happen;
Algorithms – creating clear sequences of instructions;
Decomposition – breaking larger problems into manageable parts;
Patterns – identifying similarities and using them to solve problems;
Abstraction – focusing upon the information that matters; and
Evaluation – considering whether a solution works and how it could be improved.
These skills extend far beyond the Computing lesson and help children become confident and resilient problem-solvers.
Computer Science
Computer science helps children understand how computers and digital systems work.
Children progressively develop their understanding of algorithms and programming, moving from simple sequences and instructions towards creating and debugging increasingly complex programs.
They learn that computers follow precise instructions and that when something does not work as expected, they can investigate why.
Programming therefore becomes an opportunity to practise reasoning, perseverance and problem-solving.
Rather than seeing mistakes as failure, children learn to debug: to identify a problem, test possibilities, make changes and try again.
Information Technology
Children learn how technology can be used to create, communicate, organise and present information.
Across their Brill journey, they use a range of digital tools and applications for different purposes and learn to make increasingly informed choices about which technology is most appropriate for a task.
They develop skills in creating and manipulating digital content and learn that technology can support creativity, communication, research and problem-solving.
As children progress, we expect them to become increasingly independent and adaptable users of technology rather than relying upon step-by-step instructions.
Digital Literacy
Being able to operate technology is only one part of being digitally literate.
Children also need to understand the opportunities, responsibilities and challenges that come with living in a connected world.
They learn to consider the reliability of information, understand that online content is created for different purposes and develop increasingly critical approaches to what they encounter digitally.
Children are encouraged to think about their digital footprint, privacy, communication and behaviour online, recognising that our expectations of kindness and respect apply just as much online as they do face-to-face.
Online Safety
Online safety is an essential and ongoing part of children’s education at Brill.
Children learn how to use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly and what to do when something online makes them uncomfortable, worried or unsure.
As children grow, teaching develops to reflect their increasing independence and the changing digital world around them.
Children learn about areas including privacy, passwords and personal information, appropriate communication, online relationships, digital footprints, reliable information and seeking help from a trusted adult.
Our aim is not to make children frightened of technology, but to give them the knowledge and confidence to make sensible decisions when using it.
Creating with Technology
We want children to understand that technology is something they can create with, not simply consume.
Computing provides opportunities for children to design, make, investigate and solve problems using digital tools.
They learn to make purposeful choices, evaluate their work and improve their digital creations.
This connects particularly strongly with the Creativity, Investigation, Processes and Change Big Ideas within Brill Horizons and enables children to apply their learning across different areas of the curriculum.
Computing Across Brill Horizons
Technology has meaningful applications throughout our wider curriculum.
Children may use digital tools to research, record, present, analyse, create and communicate, applying their computing knowledge within different contexts.
However, using a computer in another subject does not automatically constitute Computing.
Dedicated Computing teaching ensures children explicitly develop the subject knowledge, vocabulary and skills they need before applying these confidently elsewhere.
This balance enables technology to enhance learning without replacing the knowledge and experiences at the heart of other curriculum subjects.
An Inclusive Computing Curriculum
Computing is for every child at Brill.
Teaching is carefully structured and modelled, with appropriate adaptations and resources enabling pupils with SEND and additional needs to participate meaningfully.
Children are supported to break complex problems into manageable steps, while those who demonstrate secure understanding are challenged to create increasingly efficient solutions, explain their reasoning and apply their knowledge in unfamiliar contexts.
We want all children to develop the confidence to approach unfamiliar technology and think:
“I can work this out.”
IMPACT
By the end of their Brill journey, we want our children to be confident, creative, critical and responsible digital citizens.
We want children to leave Brill able to:
Most importantly, we want children to leave Brill understanding that technology is a powerful tool – and that how they choose to use it matters.
We want them to have the knowledge to understand it, the curiosity to explore it, the creativity to make things with it and the judgement to use it wisely.
In a world where technology will continue to change rapidly, we cannot prepare children for every piece of technology they will encounter.
We can prepare them to think, question, adapt and learn.
Be Bold. Be Brave. Be Brill-iant.

Forest School
What does Forest School look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, Forest School provides children with opportunities to explore, discover, take appropriate risks and develop confidence in the natural world.
Our beautiful rural location gives us a wonderful environment in which to extend learning beyond the classroom. Through regular Forest School experiences, children learn within an ever-changing natural environment where curiosity, imagination and adventure are encouraged.
Forest School enriches our Brill Horizons curriculum, providing opportunities for children to apply and deepen their learning while developing important personal qualities including resilience, independence, collaboration, creativity and determination.
Children explore, create, investigate, solve problems and learn practical skills. They experience the changing seasons, learn to use tools safely, develop an understanding of appropriate risk and grow in their respect and care for the natural world.
We head outdoors in almost all weathers. Children might find themselves building shelters, getting muddy, exploring woodland, tackling hills on a hot summer day – or, very occasionally, building an igloo!
Adventure is an important part of Forest School, but children’s safety, enjoyment and wellbeing are always at its heart.
INTENT
Our Forest School provision is designed to give Brill children meaningful opportunities to learn in, through and about the natural world.
We want children to experience an environment with different possibilities and boundaries from the classroom – somewhere they can explore ideas, make decisions, encounter manageable challenges and discover what they are capable of.
Through Forest School, we aim to develop:
Forest School also gives children opportunities to experience success in different ways.
For some children, particularly those who may find aspects of classroom-based learning more challenging, the outdoor environment can provide a powerful opportunity to discover strengths, build confidence and experience achievement.
We want children to be bold in exploring, brave in facing new challenges and Brill-iant in caring for each other and the world around them.

IMPLEMENTATION
Learning Beyond the Classroom
Forest School takes learning beyond the school building and into our local natural environment.
Children experience the woodland and the journey to it across different seasons and weather conditions, giving them first-hand experiences that cannot be replicated within a classroom.
Sessions combine opportunities for child-led exploration and play with carefully planned activities and challenges.
This balance allows children to follow their own curiosity while also developing specific knowledge, practical skills and personal qualities over time.
Connecting with Brill Horizons
Forest School enriches our wider Brill Horizons curriculum.
Forest School leaders work alongside class teachers to identify meaningful opportunities to connect outdoor experiences with children’s learning.
Science and Geography have particularly natural links as children observe seasonal change, investigate habitats, encounter plants and wildlife and explore their local environment.
There are also opportunities to draw upon learning in Art, Design & Technology, Mathematics and English, alongside the wider development of communication, teamwork and problem-solving.
These connections are purposeful: Forest School is not simply classroom learning moved outdoors. The natural environment provides different experiences, questions and possibilities for learning.
Exploration, Challenge and Appropriate Risk
An important part of Forest School is giving children opportunities to encounter challenge and appropriate risk within a carefully managed environment.
Children may use tools, build structures, negotiate uneven terrain or decide how to approach a practical problem.
They are taught how to assess situations, follow safety expectations and gradually take greater responsibility for themselves and others.
Rather than removing every challenge, adults support children to develop the judgement and confidence needed to manage challenges safely.
Children learn that they may not succeed immediately – and that trying again, adapting an idea and asking for help are all important parts of learning.
Independence, Collaboration and Confidence
Forest School provides rich opportunities for personal development.
Children learn to make decisions, solve problems and take increasing responsibility for their own learning.
At other times, success depends upon working together.
Building, exploring and solving practical challenges require children to communicate, negotiate, listen, share ideas and support one another.
Over time, children develop greater confidence in their own abilities and learn that their contribution can make a difference to a group.
These are skills that children can carry back into the classroom and beyond the school gates.
Caring for Our Natural World
Our rural setting gives Brill children a wonderful opportunity to develop a genuine relationship with the natural world.
Children learn to notice changes in their surroundings, observe plants and wildlife and consider the impact their actions can have upon the environment.
Our value of Compassion extends to the way we care for the world around us.
Through repeated experiences outdoors, we want children to develop not simply knowledge of nature, but respect, responsibility and a desire to protect it.
An Inclusive Forest School
Forest School is for every child at Brill.
Activities are planned with individual children’s needs in mind and adapted where necessary so that all pupils, including those with SEND and additional needs, can participate meaningfully.
The outdoor environment provides different ways to communicate, collaborate, solve problems and demonstrate success.
Children are encouraged to challenge themselves from their own starting point, developing confidence and independence over time.
There is no single way to succeed at Forest School.

Through their Forest School experiences, we want our children to become confident, curious, resilient and responsible learners.
We want children to develop:
Most importantly, we want children to transfer these qualities beyond Forest School.
The child who discovers that they can persevere with a difficult practical challenge can bring that resilience back into the classroom. The child who learns to contribute confidently to a team can carry that confidence into other areas of school life.
Forest School gives our children space to explore, get muddy, take a few carefully managed risks, discover what they can do and experience the joy of being outdoors.
It is another way in which we seek to give every Brill child the wind in their sails and the opportunity to live life in all its fullness.

History
What does History look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, we believe that History helps children understand the world they live in by understanding the people, events and ideas that shaped it.
We want children to be fascinated by the past, curious about the lives of people who came before them and confident in asking questions about how we know what happened and why different interpretations of the past may exist.
History forms part of our Brill Horizons curriculum and is supported by Cornerstones Maestro, providing a carefully sequenced progression of historical knowledge and skills from the Early Years through to Year 6.
Throughout their journey at Brill, children build an increasingly secure understanding of chronology, change, cause and consequence, similarity and difference, and historical significance, while learning to think and enquire like historians.
INTENT
Our History curriculum is ambitious for every child.
We want children to develop a coherent understanding of the past, rather than seeing History simply as a collection of unrelated periods, people and events.
Children progressively build knowledge of British, local and world history, developing an understanding of how societies have changed over time and how events and people from the past continue to influence the world in which we live today.
Our curriculum develops both:
Substantive knowledge – what children know about the past, including people, places, events, periods and societies;
Disciplinary knowledge – how historians investigate and interpret the past using evidence, enquiry and historical reasoning.
Through our History curriculum, we aim for children to:
We want children to understand that History is not simply about remembering dates. It is about asking questions, examining evidence, considering different perspectives and using what we know to make sense of the past.
Our children are encouraged to be bold in asking questions, brave in challenging assumptions and Brill-iant in using evidence to explain their thinking.

IMPLEMENTATION
Brill Horizons and Cornerstones Maestro
History is taught through our Brill Horizons curriculum, supported by Cornerstones Maestro.
Learning is carefully sequenced so that children’s historical knowledge and understanding build progressively from their earliest experiences of past and present in the Early Years through to increasingly complex historical study in Key Stage 2.
Children revisit important concepts throughout their time at Brill, allowing them to connect new learning with what they already know.
Our Brill Horizons Big Ideas provide further opportunities to make these connections. In History, children frequently explore concepts including Humankind, Change, Significance, Comparison, Processes and Place and Space.
This helps children understand that historical knowledge is connected and that the events and societies they study form part of a much bigger story.
Building Chronological Understanding
Chronology is fundamental to understanding History.
From children’s earliest understanding of past and present, we progressively develop their ability to place people, events and periods within an increasingly secure chronological framework.
Children learn to use dates and historical vocabulary appropriately and develop an understanding of duration, sequence and concurrence.
As their knowledge grows, children are encouraged to make connections between periods they have previously studied and new learning.
This allows them to understand what was happening when, how periods relate to one another and how societies and ideas have changed over time.
Our aim is that children develop an increasingly coherent mental timeline of the past onto which new historical knowledge can be placed.
Historical Enquiry
We want children to learn not only what happened, but how we know.
Children encounter a range of historical sources and learn to use them to ask and answer questions about the past.
Depending upon their age, children may explore:
As they progress through the school, children learn to consider what a source can tell us, what it cannot tell us and why evidence needs to be considered carefully.
They begin to understand that historians construct accounts of the past by examining, questioning and interpreting evidence.

Thinking Like a Historian
Historical thinking is explicitly developed throughout our curriculum.
Children learn to consider:
Change and continuity – What changed? What stayed the same?
Cause and consequence – Why did something happen? What happened as a result?
Similarity and difference – How were people’s experiences alike or different?
Significance – Why do we remember particular people, events or developments?
Evidence – How do we know?
Interpretation – Why might people describe or understand the past differently?
As children progress through Brill, they are expected to draw upon an increasingly rich body of knowledge when answering these questions and to support their ideas with historical evidence and reasoning.
Knowledge and Vocabulary
Secure knowledge is essential if children are to think deeply about History.
Important historical knowledge and vocabulary are explicitly taught, revisited and connected to previous learning.
Children develop increasingly precise use of terms relating both to the periods they study and to historical thinking itself.
Teachers support children in retrieving prior knowledge and making connections so that learning is remembered rather than simply encountered.
This enables children to discuss and write about History with increasing confidence, accuracy and sophistication.
Local History – Making the Most of Brill
Our location provides wonderful opportunities for children to understand that history exists all around them.
Brill and the surrounding area provide a rich local context through which children can explore how places and communities develop and change over time.
Our village, local landscape, buildings and landmarks – including our distinctive Brill Windmill – provide opportunities for children to connect the history they encounter in the classroom with the physical evidence of the past on their doorstep.
Where appropriate, local history is used to help children recognise connections between their own community and the wider historical story.
We want children to develop curiosity about the place in which they live and understand that History isn’t something that only happened somewhere else – they are surrounded by it.
Bringing History to Life
We want History to be memorable.
Where appropriate, children’s learning is enriched through artefacts, visitors, workshops, historical sources, trips and experiences which allow them to engage more deeply with the periods they study.
High-quality texts and carefully chosen resources help children explore the lives and perspectives of people from the past.
These experiences support knowledge rather than replacing it, helping children to visualise, question and connect with their learning.
Diverse Histories and Perspectives
History provides important opportunities for children to encounter lives and experiences beyond their own.
Throughout their time at Brill, children explore a range of societies, individuals and perspectives and consider how experiences of the past differed according to factors such as place, culture, circumstance and historical period.
We want children to recognise that History contains many voices and that our understanding becomes richer when we consider whose experiences are represented and whose may be less visible within the historical record.
This encourages children to approach the past with curiosity, thoughtfulness and respect.
An Inclusive History Curriculum
History is for every child at Brill.
Teachers use appropriate adaptations, vocabulary support, visual resources, artefacts and carefully structured learning to enable all pupils, including those with SEND and additional needs, to access important historical knowledge and concepts.
Children who demonstrate secure understanding are challenged to make increasingly sophisticated connections, evaluate evidence, consider different interpretations and construct well-reasoned historical arguments.
Our ambition is for every child to experience success while being challenged to think deeply about the past.
History Across Brill Horizons
History connects naturally with many areas of our wider curriculum.
Children use their English skills to read historical information, discuss evidence and communicate their understanding. Geography helps children understand how place and environment influence societies, while Art, RE and other subjects provide further insight into the beliefs, creativity and experiences of people from different times and places.
Through Brill Horizons, children are encouraged to recognise these connections.

Mathematics
What does Maths look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, we believe that every child can become a confident and successful mathematician.
Mathematics is essential for understanding and engaging with the world around us. But Maths is about far more than getting the right answer. We want our children to notice, question, explore, make connections, explain their thinking and persevere when something is challenging.
Our approach is based upon the principles of teaching for mastery and is supported by White Rose Maths. In addition, Mastering Number strengthens children’s early number sense and fluency, providing secure foundations upon which future mathematical learning can be built.
Throughout their Brill journey, children develop:
Fluency – knowing, recalling and using mathematics efficientlyReasoning – explaining, connecting and justifying mathematical thinkingProblem Solving – applying knowledge to increasingly complex and unfamiliar situations
A strong understanding of the fundamentals of mathematics underpins all three.
INTENT
Our Maths curriculum is ambitious for every child.
We believe that secure mathematical foundations matter. Children need a deep understanding of number, alongside increasingly automatic recall of important facts, if they are to confidently access more complex mathematics as they progress through school.
Developing these fundamentals is therefore a particular priority at Brill.
We want children to develop strong number sense, understand the relationships between numbers and operations and become increasingly fluent in recalling and applying key number facts.
Our curriculum aims to ensure that children:
Most importantly, we want children to develop a positive mathematical identity.
We want Brill children to believe that mathematics is something they can do. Mistakes are welcomed as part of learning, different strategies are explored and children are encouraged to have a go even when they are unsure.
Our children are encouraged to be bold in exploring ideas, brave when facing challenge and Brill-iant in explaining their mathematical thinking.

IMPLEMENTATION
Teaching for Mastery – White Rose Maths
Maths is taught daily through a mastery approach, supported by White Rose Maths.
Learning is carefully sequenced so that new mathematical knowledge builds upon secure prior understanding. Concepts are broken into manageable steps, allowing children to develop understanding before moving on to increasingly complex applications.
Teachers use questioning, modelling, mathematical discussion and carefully selected representations to uncover children’s thinking and identify misconceptions.
Importantly, learning is regularly revisited.
Children retrieve and apply previously taught knowledge so that important mathematical facts, concepts and procedures are not simply learned for a lesson or unit but remembered and available when children need them.
Building Strong Foundations – Mastering Number
In the early stages of children’s mathematical development, we place particular emphasis on developing strong number sense.
Mastering Number complements our wider Maths curriculum by providing regular opportunities for children to develop fluency and flexibility with number.
Children learn to notice relationships, recognise quantities, compose and decompose numbers and develop increasingly efficient ways of calculating.
Rather than relying upon counting or memorised procedures alone, children develop a deeper understanding of how numbers work and how they relate to one another.
These strong foundations are crucial. When children have secure number sense and can recall key facts automatically, they have greater capacity to tackle the more complex reasoning and problem-solving they encounter later in their mathematical journey.
Securing the Fundamentals
Across Brill, we are placing a particularly strong emphasis on ensuring that children have the fundamental mathematical knowledge they need to succeed.
Teachers use assessment and their knowledge of individual pupils to identify gaps in foundational knowledge and address these before they become barriers to future learning.
Children are given regular opportunities to retrieve, revisit and practise essential knowledge, including:
This does not mean mathematics becomes repetitive or simply about memorising facts.
Instead, we want children to develop the right balance of automaticity and understanding – knowing important facts quickly while also understanding the mathematical relationships behind them.
Our aim is simple: secure the foundations so that every child is ready for what comes next.

Multiplication and Times Tables – Years 3 and 4
As children move into Key Stage 2, multiplication and division become an important mathematical priority, with a particular focus in Years 3 and 4.
Secure times-table knowledge unlocks a significant amount of later mathematics. It supports children’s understanding of division, fractions, ratio, area and more complex calculation, while reducing the cognitive load involved in solving increasingly challenging problems.
We therefore provide frequent opportunities for children to learn, practise, retrieve and apply multiplication and related division facts.
In Year 3, children build increasingly secure multiplication knowledge and develop an understanding of the patterns and relationships within and between times tables.
In Year 4, this knowledge is strengthened further, with the aim that children can recall multiplication and corresponding division facts accurately, confidently and with increasing automaticity.
Our approach goes beyond simply learning a sequence of answers. Children explore patterns, make connections, use known facts to derive unknown facts and develop strategies that help multiplication facts become secure and meaningful.
By making multiplication knowledge a strong and consistent focus, we aim to give children the fluency they need to confidently access mathematics throughout Key Stage 2 and beyond.
Concrete, Pictorial, Abstract – CPA
A key feature of our mastery approach is the use of Concrete, Pictorial and Abstract (CPA) representations.
Children encounter mathematical concepts in different ways:
Concrete – using practical equipment and manipulatives to explore mathematical ideas.
Pictorial – representing mathematics through images, diagrams and models.
Abstract – using mathematical symbols, notation and calculations.
These are not simply stages that children ‘grow out of’. Appropriate representations are used throughout the school to help children see mathematics, make connections and explain their thinking.
Manipulatives and representations such as counters, tens frames, number lines, part-whole models, arrays and bar models help children develop conceptual understanding alongside increasingly efficient abstract methods.
Fluency
Fluency is a fundamental part of becoming a successful mathematician.
Children are given regular opportunities to practise and retrieve important number facts, mathematical knowledge and calculation strategies.
We want children to develop accuracy, efficiency and flexibility. This means knowing facts automatically where appropriate, but also being able to select an efficient strategy and adapt their thinking.
As children’s automatic recall develops, less working memory is required for basic calculations, enabling them to concentrate on the more complex mathematical thinking involved in reasoning and problem solving.
Reasoning and Mathematical Talk
Children are taught not simply to give an answer, but to explain how they know.
Mathematical talk is an important feature of lessons. Teachers model precise mathematical vocabulary and children are encouraged to articulate their thinking, compare approaches and listen to the reasoning of others.
By explaining their mathematics, children deepen their own understanding and learn that successful mathematicians think about the relationships between numbers rather than simply carrying out procedures.

make and test conjectures;
compare and classify;
explain their chosen strategy;
identify and correct errors;
prove or justify their thinking; and
use mathematical vocabulary accurately.
Problem Solving
Problem solving enables children to apply their knowledge in situations where the method or answer may not immediately be obvious.
Children encounter problems in a range of contexts and learn how to identify the mathematics required, select an appropriate strategy and break more complex problems into manageable steps.
We encourage children to embrace productive struggle – to think, explore, try a different approach and persevere rather than expecting every answer to come immediately.
In doing so, children develop independence, resilience and confidence.
Challenge and Support
We are ambitious for every mathematician at Brill.
Children work towards the same important mathematical concepts, with teachers carefully adapting teaching, representations, scaffolds and resources so that all pupils can access and understand the learning.
Where children have gaps in fundamental knowledge, these are identified and addressed quickly through additional teaching, practice and opportunities for retrieval.
Children who grasp concepts rapidly are challenged through greater depth – applying their knowledge in increasingly complex situations, making connections, reasoning and proving – rather than simply racing ahead to new curriculum content.
This allows every child to experience both success and appropriate challenge.
Maths Across Brill Horizons
Mathematics does not exist only within the Maths lesson.
Through our wider Brill Horizons curriculum, children have opportunities to apply mathematical knowledge in meaningful contexts.
They may collect and interpret data in science, explore chronology in history, work with scale and coordinates in geography, measure and calculate in design and technology or investigate pattern and proportion through art.
Children are also encouraged to recognise mathematics in everyday life – including money, time, measurement, travel, sport and the many decisions and problems we encounter beyond school.
These connections help children understand that mathematics is not simply something they do at school; it is a powerful way of understanding and navigating the world.
IMPACT
By the end of their Brill journey, we want our children to see themselves as capable, confident and resilient mathematicians.
We want children to leave Brill able to:
Most importantly, we want children to leave Brill believing:
demonstrate strong conceptual understanding;

“I can do maths.”
Successful mathematicians are not simply those who calculate quickly. They are those who notice, think, question, connect, explain and persevere.
By securing strong mathematical foundations from the very beginning and building upon them throughout each child’s journey, we aim to ensure that every Brill child has the knowledge, confidence and curiosity they need for their next stage of education and for life beyond our school.

PE
What does PE look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, we believe that Physical Education plays an essential role in helping children to become healthy, confident, resilient and active young people.
We want every child to experience the enjoyment of being physically active and to develop the skills, knowledge and confidence they need to participate in physical activity throughout their lives.
Our PE provision combines specialist expertise with high-quality class teacher-led PE. Every child receives two hours of curriculum PE each week: one hour delivered by specialist coaches from Premier Education and one hour taught by their class teacher.
Our facilities and local environment further enrich our provision. Children benefit from our school grounds, access to the MUGA adjacent to the school and the local playing fields, as well as the particularly special opportunity to learn to swim in our own school swimming pool.
Through PE, we encourage children to be bold in trying something new, brave when facing physical challenge and Brill-iant in supporting themselves and others to succeed.
INTENT
Our PE curriculum is ambitious and inclusive for every child.
We want children to develop the physical competence, confidence and motivation to lead healthy and active lives.
Through a broad range of physical activities, children develop fundamental movement skills before applying and refining these within increasingly challenging individual and team activities.
Our PE curriculum aims to enable children to:
We recognise that children’s experiences of sport and physical activity outside school vary considerably. Our role is therefore to ensure that every child has opportunities to participate, develop and experience success.
become increasingly confident and physically literate;
understand and apply rules, tactics and strategies;
communicate and collaborate with others;
develop safe and confident swimming skills; and
IMPLEMENTATION
Two Hours of PE Every Week
Children receive two hours of curriculum PE each week.
One hour is delivered by specialist coaches from Premier Education, bringing additional expertise and high-quality specialist provision into school.
The second hour is taught by the child’s class teacher, providing continuity and enabling teachers to build upon children’s previous learning and development.
This combination of specialist and teacher-led provision gives children regular opportunities to practise, apply and refine their physical skills across a broad range of activities.
Developing Physical Literacy
Our curriculum develops children’s physical skills progressively throughout their time at Brill.
In the early stages, there is a strong emphasis on developing fundamental movement skills, including balance, coordination, agility, running, jumping, throwing and catching.
As children progress through the school, these foundations are increasingly applied within different sports and physical activities.
Children learn not only how to perform skills, but how to select and apply them effectively. They develop an increasing understanding of movement, rules, tactics, teamwork and decision-making.
Through demonstration, practice, feedback and opportunities to refine performance, children learn that physical competence develops through practice, perseverance and reflection.
Swimming at Brill
Swimming is a particularly special part of our PE offer.
We are incredibly fortunate to have our own outdoor swimming pool on the school site, allowing children to develop their swimming skills within the familiar environment of Brill School.
Swimming lessons take place during the later spring and summer terms and are delivered by a member of our school staff who is also a qualified swimming instructor.
Children are taught to become increasingly confident, competent and safe in the water, developing appropriate swimming strokes, stamina and water-safety skills.
Having our own pool enables swimming to be a genuine part of school life and gives our children valuable opportunities to develop an important life skill.

Making the Most of Our Environment
Our location allows us to extend PE beyond the immediate school site.
Alongside our school grounds, we have access to the MUGA located just outside the school, providing an additional dedicated space for physical activity.
Where activities require a larger space, children also make use of the local playing fields.
These facilities enable us to offer children a varied PE experience and select spaces appropriate to the activity being taught.
Teamwork, Character and Our Values
PE provides powerful opportunities for personal development.
Children learn to work with different people, communicate effectively, take responsibility and understand the importance of their contribution to a team.
They experience success and disappointment and learn how to respond appropriately to both.
Our Christian values are naturally reflected through PE:
Honesty – playing fairly and taking responsibility for our actions.
Hope – believing that improvement is possible and continuing to work towards our goals.
Courage – trying something unfamiliar, taking appropriate risks and persevering when something feels difficult.
Compassion – encouraging others, showing respect and recognising that everybody has different strengths.
We want children to understand that how we participate matters just as much as whether we win.
Competition and Opportunity
Competition provides children with opportunities to apply their skills, challenge themselves and represent their school.
Through appropriate competitive experiences, children learn about teamwork, determination, fair play, resilience and respect.
We want competition to be a positive experience in which children can strive to do their best while learning to celebrate the achievements of others.
Alongside competition, we value participation and want children to experience a range of activities so that they have opportunities to discover something they enjoy and feel successful doing.
An Inclusive PE Curriculum
PE is for every child at Brill.
Teachers and specialist coaches adapt activities, equipment, groupings and levels of challenge where appropriate so that all pupils, including children with SEND and additional needs, can participate meaningfully and experience success.
Children who demonstrate greater confidence or competence are challenged to refine their technique, make increasingly sophisticated tactical decisions, take greater responsibility and support the learning of others.
Our aim is for every child to leave a PE lesson feeling that they have participated, progressed and been challenged appropriately.
PE Across Brill Horizons
Physical Education contributes significantly to our wider Brill Horizons curriculum and to children’s personal development.
PE teaches children about their bodies, health and wellbeing while developing attributes that support learning throughout school: resilience, independence, communication, cooperation, determination and courage.
Children learn that looking after their physical health is an important part of living life to the full.
Our PE provision therefore supports our wider aspiration to develop children who are confident, ambitious and ready to embrace the opportunities available to them.
IMPACT
By the end of their Brill journey, we want our children to see themselves as capable, confident and active individuals.

Most importantly, we want every child to leave Brill understanding that being active is for everyone.
Whether their passion becomes competitive sport, swimming, dance, walking, fitness or simply enjoying being outdoors, we want our children to have the confidence, skills and positive experiences that encourage them to remain active throughout their lives.

RE
What does RE look like at Brill?
At Brill Church of England School, Religious Education is a valued and important part of our curriculum and our identity as a Church of England school.
Our Christian vision,
“With the wind in our sails, we shall live ‘life in all its fullness’.” (John 10:10)
shapes the life of our school and our aspiration for every child to flourish academically, socially, emotionally and spiritually.
Through RE, we want children to develop a rich understanding of Christianity as a living and diverse world faith, while also encountering a range of other religions and worldviews. Children are encouraged to ask meaningful questions, explore different beliefs and perspectives and reflect thoughtfully upon their own ideas and experiences.
Our RE curriculum is supported by Jigsaw/Discovery RE, providing an enquiry-based approach that places questions, discussion, knowledge and reflection at the heart of learning.
Our close relationship with All Saints Church in Brill and the wider church community further enriches children’s experiences, enabling them to encounter Christianity as something that is both studied in the classroom and lived within their local community.
We want RE to be a subject in which children can think deeply, ask big questions and engage respectfully with ideas that may be different from their own.
INTENT
Our RE curriculum is ambitious for every child.
We want children to develop secure knowledge and understanding of Christianity and a range of religions and worldviews, while developing the ability to question, interpret, compare, reflect and form thoughtful responses.
RE provides children with opportunities to explore some of life’s biggest questions:
What do people believe?Why do they believe it?How does belief influence the way people live?What does it mean to belong?How do people understand God and the world?What can we learn from one another?
Through our RE curriculum, we aim for children to:
RE at Brill is not about telling children what to believe.
It provides children with the knowledge and space to explore what people believe, why those beliefs matter and how faith and worldview can shape the way people understand and experience the world.
We encourage children to be bold in asking big questions, brave in exploring different ideas and Brill-iant in listening, thinking and responding with respect.
develop secure knowledge and understanding of Christianity;
ask increasingly thoughtful theological and philosophical questions;
consider different interpretations and perspectives;

IMPLEMENTATION
Jigsaw / Discovery RE
Our Religious Education curriculum is supported by Jigsaw/Discovery RE, providing a structured and progressive enquiry-based approach to RE from the Early Years through to Year 6.
Big questions and enquiry sit at the heart of learning.
Children are encouraged to explore ideas, develop relevant knowledge and consider how beliefs are understood and expressed within different religions and worldviews.
Through this approach, children develop both their religious knowledge and their ability to think deeply about belief.
Enquiries provide opportunities for children to:
This enquiry approach means that RE at Brill is not simply about remembering facts about different religions.
Children are expected to use what they know to think, question, compare, interpret and respond.
As children progress through the school, they revisit important concepts and encounter increasingly sophisticated questions, enabling their knowledge and understanding to deepen over time.
